Nature changes too slowly
qs.why: “landscapes… have been shaped by humans for thousands of years and there is no single natural state to return to.”

qs.q: What does the final sentence suggest?
qs.a: Success depends on winning people's support
w: Nature does not need human help at all
People should not live near rewilded areas
Rewilding projects should be kept secret
qs.why: “Nature may be able to look after itself, but people still need to be persuaded to let it.”

items.title: Should We Trust Online Reviews?
items.tvi: Có nên tin nhận xét trên mạng?
items.text:
Before booking a hotel, choosing a restaurant or buying a kettle, most of us now consult the opinions of strangers. Online reviews have become one of the most influential forces in modern consumer life, and their appeal is easy to understand. Unlike advertising, they seem to offer the honest views of ordinary people with no reason to deceive.
That assumption, unfortunately, is not always justified. Fake reviews, written by businesses about themselves or by paid agencies, are a persistent problem, and investigations have repeatedly uncovered networks offering five-star ratings for a fee. Some sellers offer refunds or free products to customers who leave positive comments, a practice that is banned on many platforms but difficult to detect.
Even genuine reviews present a distorted picture. People are far more likely to write a review after an unusually good or unusually bad experience than after an ordinary one, so ratings tend to cluster at the extremes. Early reviews also carry disproportionate weight: a product that receives a few enthusiastic comments in its first weeks may attract more buyers, who in turn leave more positive reviews, regardless of whether it is genuinely better than its competitors.
There is, moreover, the question of what a rating actually measures. A one-star review of a restaurant may reflect a long wait on a busy evening, a misunderstanding about the menu, or simply a bad mood. Researchers who analysed thousands of hotel reviews found that a substantial share of negative comments concerned factors outside the hotel's control, such as the weather or noisy neighbours.
Platforms have responded with verification systems and algorithms designed to identify suspicious patterns, and in some countries regulators have begun to fine companies that publish fake reviews. These measures help, but they are unlikely to solve the problem entirely, because the incentives to manipulate ratings remain strong.
For consumers, the sensible approach is neither blind trust nor complete cynicism. Reading a range of reviews, paying attention to specific details rather than star ratings, and treating both extremes with some suspicion can help separate useful information from noise. Reviews, in other words, are best read the way one might listen to advice from a crowd: worth hearing, but not to be followed without thinking.

qs.q: Why, according to the writer, do people find online reviews appealing?
qs.a: They seem more honest than advertising
w: They are written by experts
They are always up to date
They are checked by the government
qs.why: “Unlike advertising, they seem to offer the honest views of ordinary people with no reason to deceive.”

qs.q: Why do ratings tend to “cluster at the extremes”?
qs.a: People mostly write reviews after very good or very bad experiences
w: Platforms delete average reviews
Most products are either excellent or terrible
Customers are paid to give extreme ratings
qs.why: “far more likely to write a review after an unusually good or unusually bad experience.”

qs.q: What problem with early reviews is described?
qs.a: They can influence later sales and ratings too strongly
w: They are usually written by the seller
They are often deleted by platforms
They are less detailed than later reviews
qs.why: “Early reviews also carry disproportionate weight… regardless of whether it is genuinely better.”

qs.q: What did the analysis of hotel reviews show?
qs.a: Many complaints concerned things hotels could not control
w: Most reviews were fake
Negative reviews were usually accurate
Guests rarely mentioned the weather
qs.why: “a substantial share of negative comments concerned factors outside the hotel's control.”

qs.q: Why does the writer think platform measures will not solve the problem completely?
qs.a: There are still strong reasons for businesses to cheat
w: The algorithms are too expensive
Regulators refuse to act
Consumers do not read reviews
qs.why: “because the incentives to manipulate ratings remain strong.”

qs.q: What does the comparison with “advice from a crowd” suggest?
qs.a: Reviews should be considered critically, not simply obeyed
w: Reviews should be ignored completely
Popular products are always the best
Only negative reviews are reliable
qs.why: “worth hearing, but not to be followed without thinking.”

items.title: The Placebo Puzzle
items.tvi: Câu đố về thuốc giả
items.text:
For most of the twentieth century, the placebo effect was regarded as a nuisance – something to be eliminated from drug trials so that the 'real' effect of a medicine could be measured. Patients who improved after taking a sugar pill were assumed to have imagined their recovery, or to have been on the mend anyway.
That view now looks too simple. Brain-imaging studies have shown that when people expect pain relief, their brains release natural painkillers, so the relief they report is not merely imaginary. Expectation, it turns out, can produce measurable changes in the body, particularly for symptoms such as pain, nausea and fatigue.
Stranger still are experiments with so-called 'open-label' placebos, in which patients are told quite frankly that the pills they are taking contain no active ingredient. In several small trials, people with chronic back pain or digestive disorders still reported improvements. Researchers suspect that the ritual of treatment – the consultation, the instructions, the act of taking something regularly – may matter as much as the pill itself.
None of this means that placebos can shrink tumours or cure infections; there is no good evidence that they can. But it does suggest that the way medicine is delivered – how much time a doctor spends listening, how a treatment is explained – may influence outcomes far more than we once assumed.

qs.q: How was the placebo effect viewed in the past?
qs.a: As something that got in the way of testing drugs
w: As a useful treatment for pain
As proof that most medicines did not work
qs.why: “regarded as a nuisance – something to be eliminated from drug trials”

qs.q: What did brain-imaging studies show?
qs.a: Expecting relief can cause real physical changes
w: Patients usually imagine their improvement
Placebos work better than painkillers
qs.why: “their brains release natural painkillers, so the relief they report is not merely imaginary.”

qs.q: What is surprising about 'open-label' placebos?
qs.a: They seem to help even when patients know they are fake
w: They are more expensive than real drugs
They only work for serious diseases
qs.why: “told quite frankly that the pills… contain no active ingredient… still reported improvements.”

qs.q: What does the writer suggest in the final paragraph?
qs.a: How care is given may affect how patients recover
w: Placebos could replace many medicines
Doctors should prescribe sugar pills more often
qs.why: “the way medicine is delivered… may influence outcomes far more than we once assumed.”

items.title: The Economics of Queuing
items.tvi: Kinh tế học của việc xếp hàng
items.text:
Nobody enjoys waiting in line, yet queues are one of the oldest ways of sharing out something scarce. Unlike prices, which favour those with money, a queue favours those with time – a principle many people regard as fairer, even if it is hardly efficient.
Economists have long pointed out the hidden cost. An hour spent waiting for concert tickets is an hour not spent working, studying or resting, and the value of that lost time is rarely counted. In theory, auctioning the tickets would be more efficient: they would go to those willing to pay most. In practice, the idea provokes outrage, because it appears to turn a fan's enthusiasm into a privilege of wealth.
Businesses have found ways to profit from this tension. Theme parks sell 'fast passes' that allow visitors to skip the line; airlines offer priority boarding. Each innovation is defended as offering customers choice, but critics argue that it quietly converts a shared, if irritating, experience into a two-tier system.
Psychologists add another twist: how long a wait feels matters more than how long it actually is. Unoccupied time seems longer than occupied time, uncertain waits seem longer than known ones, and unfair waits – when someone pushes in – are the most frustrating of all. This is why some airports have deliberately made passengers walk further to collect their luggage: the walk feels like progress, whereas standing at an empty carousel feels like waiting.

qs.q: Why do many people think queues are fairer than prices?
qs.a: They do not depend on how much money people have
w: They are the most efficient system
They reward people who arrive in groups
qs.why: “Unlike prices, which favour those with money, a queue favours those with time”

qs.q: Why does auctioning tickets cause anger?
qs.a: It seems to give wealthy people an advantage
w: It takes longer than queuing
It is harder to organise
qs.why: “it appears to turn a fan's enthusiasm into a privilege of wealth.”

qs.q: What do critics say about 'fast passes'?
qs.a: They create two classes of customer
w: They make queues move faster for everyone
They are too expensive to be popular
qs.why: “converts a shared, if irritating, experience into a two-tier system.”

qs.q: Why might an airport make passengers walk further?
qs.a: Walking makes the wait feel shorter
w: It reduces crowding at the carousel
It helps passengers find the right exit
qs.why: “the walk feels like progress, whereas standing at an empty carousel feels like waiting.”

items.title: When Languages Fall Silent
items.tvi: Khi một ngôn ngữ im tiếng
items.text:
Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that around half may disappear by the end of this century. Most are spoken by small communities, and many are no longer being learnt by children – the clearest sign that a language is in danger.
Why should the rest of us care? One answer is scientific. Each language encodes a different way of organising experience: some have no words for 'left' and 'right' and describe space entirely in terms of compass directions; others mark in their grammar whether the speaker witnessed an event or merely heard about it. When a language vanishes before it has been recorded, that evidence of human possibility is lost for good.
For speakers, however, the loss is rarely abstract. Language carries songs, place names, jokes and knowledge of local plants that may exist nowhere else. People who have lost their ancestral language often describe it as losing a connection to their grandparents.
Revival is difficult but not impossible. Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly in religious texts, became the everyday language of millions. Welsh has gained speakers through schools that teach entirely in the language, and Māori has been revived partly through 'language nests', where young children are cared for by fluent elders. What these cases share is not money or technology alone, but a community that decides the language is worth passing on.

qs.q: According to the text, what most clearly shows that a language is in danger?
qs.a: Children are no longer learning it
w: It has no written form
It is spoken in only one country
qs.why: “many are no longer being learnt by children – the clearest sign that a language is in danger.”

qs.q: Why does the writer mention compass directions?
qs.a: To show that languages organise experience differently
w: To explain how languages spread
To show that some languages are more precise
qs.why: “Each language encodes a different way of organising experience”

qs.q: How do people often describe losing their ancestral language?
qs.a: As losing a link to earlier generations
w: As a purely scientific loss
As something that happens without pain
qs.why: “losing a connection to their grandparents.”

qs.q: What do successful revivals have in common, according to the writer?
qs.a: A community determined to keep the language alive
w: Large amounts of government money
Modern technology such as apps
qs.why: “a community that decides the language is worth passing on.”

items.title: The Rise of Slow Travel
items.tvi: Du lịch chậm lên ngôi
items.text:
For a generation raised on cheap flights, the ideal holiday often meant seeing as much as possible in as little time as possible: five cities in ten days, each one photographed and ticked off. A growing number of travellers are now rejecting that model in favour of what has been called 'slow travel'.
The principle is straightforward. Rather than racing between famous sights, slow travellers stay longer in fewer places, go by train or bus where they can, and try to live, however briefly, like residents – shopping at local markets, learning a few phrases, returning to the same café until the owner recognises them.
Part of the appeal is environmental. Flying is by far the most carbon-intensive way to travel, and a single long-haul return flight can produce more emissions than many people in poorer countries generate in a year. But advocates insist that the main reward is the experience itself: a city absorbed over a fortnight, they argue, is remembered quite differently from one glimpsed in an afternoon.
Not everyone is persuaded. Slow travel, critics note, demands something many workers simply do not have: long stretches of free time. A family with two weeks' annual leave may feel that being lectured about the virtues of a month-long train journey is a luxury of the privileged. Even its supporters admit that the movement risks becoming another lifestyle label – something to be photographed and posted, rather than practised.

qs.q: What kind of holiday does the first paragraph describe?
qs.a: One that tries to cover many places quickly
w: One spent in a single city
One that avoids famous sights
qs.why: “five cities in ten days, each one photographed and ticked off.”

qs.q: According to its advocates, what is the greatest benefit of slow travel?
qs.a: A deeper experience of places
w: Lower travel costs
Less need for planning
qs.why: “the main reward is the experience itself”

qs.q: What is the critics' chief objection?
qs.a: Many people cannot take enough time off
w: Trains are more expensive than flights
Slow travel harms local communities
qs.why: “demands something many workers simply do not have: long stretches of free time.”

qs.q: What risk do even supporters accept?
qs.a: It may become more about image than practice
w: It may become too popular for small towns
It may encourage people to fly more
qs.why: “something to be photographed and posted, rather than practised.”

items.title: Trusting Strangers
items.tvi: Niềm tin vào người lạ
items.text:
Imagine you find a wallet in the street containing a business card and some cash. Would you return it? And would you be more or less likely to do so if it contained a lot of money?
Most people, asked to predict the behaviour of others, assume that more cash means more temptation – and therefore fewer returns. Yet when researchers handed in thousands of apparently lost wallets at banks, hotels and offices in dozens of countries, they found the opposite. In most places, wallets containing money were reported to their owners more often than empty ones, and in follow-up tests, wallets with larger sums were returned more often still.
The researchers' explanation centres on self-image. Keeping an empty wallet costs a person little in terms of how they see themselves; keeping one full of someone else's money feels uncomfortably close to theft. Most people, it seems, want to be able to think of themselves as honest, and that desire can outweigh the attraction of easy money.
The findings carry a striking implication. If we routinely underestimate the honesty of strangers, we may be designing our institutions – our contracts, our checks, our surveillance – for a population less trustworthy than the one we actually live among. Excessive suspicion has costs of its own: it can insult the honest majority, and there is some evidence that being treated as untrustworthy makes people behave less honestly.

qs.q: What did most people expect to happen to wallets containing more money?
qs.a: Fewer of them would be returned
w: More of them would be returned
The amount would make no difference
qs.why: “more cash means more temptation – and therefore fewer returns.”

qs.q: Why, according to the researchers, did people return wallets with money?
qs.a: They wanted to see themselves as honest
w: They expected a reward
They were afraid of being caught
qs.why: “Most people… want to be able to think of themselves as honest”

qs.q: What does the writer suggest about our institutions?
qs.a: They may assume people are less honest than they are
w: They need more surveillance
They work well because people are honest
qs.why: “designing our institutions… for a population less trustworthy than the one we actually live among.”

qs.q: Which possible effect of excessive suspicion is mentioned?
qs.a: It may make people behave less honestly
w: It may make institutions cheaper to run
It may reduce the number of lost wallets
qs.why: “being treated as untrustworthy makes people behave less honestly.”

items.title: The Library of Things
items.tvi: Thư viện đồ dùng
items.text:
In the basement of a former bank in the fictional town of Halbrook, residents can borrow a drill, a tent or a pasta machine as easily as a novel. The 'library of things' there holds more than two thousand items, and its founders insist that the idea is less about saving money than about changing assumptions about ownership.

The logic is straightforward. The average household drill is used for a matter of minutes in its entire lifetime, yet millions are manufactured every year. Sharing such tools, advocates argue, reduces waste and frees up cupboard space. Members pay a small annual fee, and volunteers repair damaged items instead of discarding them.

Critics raise reasonable objections. Borrowing requires planning, which many people find inconvenient when a project suddenly demands a particular tool. Some retailers also worry that such schemes will erode sales, although the evidence so far is thin. A study of three similar libraries found that most members still bought equipment they used regularly, and that borrowing mainly replaced one-off purchases they would otherwise have regretted.

Perhaps the most surprising finding concerned social contact. Members who collected items in person often stayed to chat, swap advice or offer help with a task. One volunteer admitted that she had expected a service for thrifty households and found herself running something closer to a community centre. If the scheme spreads, its lasting legacy may therefore be less environmental than social: a reminder that neighbours remain a resource.

qs.q: What do the founders say about the purpose of the library?
qs.a: It is meant to change how people think about owning things
w: It is intended mainly to cut household bills
It exists to supply rare equipment to professionals
qs.why: “less about saving money than about changing assumptions about ownership.”

qs.q: What drawback of borrowing is mentioned?
qs.a: It demands advance planning
w: Borrowed tools are often returned damaged
The annual fee is too high for most people
qs.why: “Borrowing requires planning”

qs.q: What did the study of three libraries find about members?
qs.a: They kept buying things they needed often
w: They stopped buying any equipment
They bought more equipment than before
qs.why: “most members still bought equipment they used regularly”

qs.q: What does the volunteer's experience suggest?
qs.a: The scheme has turned out to serve a different purpose than expected
w: The scheme works best when staffed by professionals
The scheme should remain small to stay useful
qs.why: “expected a service for thrifty households and found herself running something closer to a community centre.”

items.title: Handwriting in a Digital Age
items.tvi: Chữ viết tay thời kỹ thuật số
items.text:
Schools in several countries have recently begun reintroducing handwriting lessons, reversing a decade in which keyboards were seen as the obvious future. The shift owes less to nostalgia than to a growing, if still modest, body of research. In one widely discussed experiment, students who took notes by hand performed better on conceptual questions than classmates who typed, apparently because writing slowly forced them to summarise rather than transcribe.

Not everyone is convinced. Several researchers point out that the original studies involved small groups, and that later attempts to repeat them produced mixed results. Typing, moreover, is faster, legible to everyone and indispensable for most careers. Teachers also note that children with motor difficulties may find pens frustrating, and that insisting on cursive can disadvantage them without any clear educational gain.

What seems clearer is that the two skills serve different purposes. Handwriting appears to help young children recognise letters, since forming a shape engages the memory in ways that pressing a key does not. Typing, on the other hand, supports fluency once the basics are secure. A sensible curriculum, one headteacher suggested, would not choose between them but sequence them: pens first, keyboards later.

Her own school adopted that approach two years ago. Parents were initially sceptical, she admits, but few have since asked for the change to be reversed. Whether the improvement in results is due to the pens, however, she cannot say; too many other things changed at the same time.

qs.q: What has prompted schools to bring back handwriting?
qs.a: Evidence from research
w: A wish to return to older traditions
Complaints from employers about typing
qs.why: “The shift owes less to nostalgia than to a growing, if still modest, body of research.”

qs.q: Why are some researchers doubtful about the early experiments?
qs.a: The studies were small and later results varied
w: The students were too young to type
The tests asked only about simple facts
qs.why: “the original studies involved small groups”

qs.q: What is said about handwriting and young children?
qs.a: It helps them learn to recognise letters
w: It makes them faster at typing later
It is useful mainly for children with motor difficulties
qs.why: “Handwriting appears to help young children recognise letters”

qs.q: What does the headteacher's final remark suggest?
qs.a: The benefits of the new approach are not proven
w: The new approach has clearly failed
Parents are likely to demand changes soon
qs.why: “Whether the improvement in results is due to the pens, however, she cannot say”

items.title: Do City Bees Help?
items.tvi: Ong thành phố có giúp ích không?
items.text:
Rooftop hives have become a fashionable symbol of green living, with companies installing them on office towers and hotels. Many people assume that every bee added to a city is a small victory for nature. Ecologists, however, are increasingly uneasy about that assumption.

The difficulty is that honeybees are managed livestock, not wild animals. A single hive can contain fifty thousand insects, all foraging within a few kilometres. In cities where flowers are limited, they may take nectar and pollen that would otherwise sustain the hundreds of native species, such as solitary bees and hoverflies, that are genuinely at risk. One survey in a large European city found that wild bees visited fewer flowers in neighbourhoods with dense clusters of hives, although the researchers cautioned that other factors might also be responsible.

None of this means beekeepers are acting in bad faith. Many are motivated by a sincere wish to help, and their hobby introduces people to the natural world. The more productive question, according to one conservation officer, is not whether to keep bees but how many a given area can support. Planting more flowers, she argues, would benefit honeybees and wild species alike, whereas simply adding hives treats the symptom rather than the cause.

For now, companies keen to advertise their environmental credentials might be better advised to fund meadows than hives, a choice that is less photogenic but arguably more effective.

qs.q: Why are ecologists uneasy about rooftop hives?
qs.a: Honeybees may use up food that wild species need
w: Honeybees spread disease to native insects
Hives attract too many insects to office buildings
qs.why: “they may take nectar and pollen that would otherwise sustain the hundreds of native species”

qs.q: Why did the researchers urge caution about their survey?
qs.a: Something else could explain the result
w: The survey covered too few flowers
The hives were not counted accurately
qs.why: “other factors might also be responsible”

qs.q: What is the conservation officer's view?
qs.a: The key issue is how many hives an area can support
w: Beekeeping should be banned in cities
Beekeepers should receive formal training
qs.why: “not whether to keep bees but how many a given area can support”

qs.q: What does the writer imply about companies that install hives?
qs.a: Their choice may be influenced by the image it creates
w: They usually have little interest in nature
They install hives without checking local laws
qs.why: “less photogenic but arguably more effective.”

items.title: The Case for Slow Journalism
items.tvi: Lập luận cho báo chí chậm
items.text:
The pressure to publish within minutes has reshaped the news. Stories are posted before facts are confirmed, corrected later and then, often, forgotten. Against this trend, a small number of outlets have embraced what they call 'slow journalism': fewer stories, published less often, but researched over months rather than hours.

Supporters argue that speed rewards the wrong qualities. A reporter who must file within the hour has little time to visit the place concerned, find sources who disagree, or admit that the story is more complicated than first appeared. The slow approach, by contrast, treats context as the product. Readers of one such magazine, for instance, are told at the outset how long an investigation took and what the reporters could not establish, a candour that is rare in conventional news.

The model has obvious limits. Subscribers are mostly well educated and comfortable financially, which raises the awkward question of who is being informed. Nor can slow methods cover an emergency, when readers need information at once. Several editors therefore describe their work as complementary rather than rival to fast news: the daily bulletin tells you what happened; the slower article attempts to explain why.

Whether that distinction will survive is uncertain. Audiences accustomed to constant updates may lack the patience for a twelve-thousand-word feature, and advertisers have shown little enthusiasm for it. Even so, the fact that anyone is willing to bet on patience in this market is itself revealing.

qs.q: What is the main aim of 'slow journalism'?
qs.a: To produce fewer, more thoroughly researched stories
w: To correct mistakes made by fast news outlets
To publish stories before rival outlets can
qs.why: “fewer stories, published less often, but researched over months rather than hours.”

qs.q: What is unusual about the magazine mentioned?
qs.a: It tells readers what it failed to find out
w: It publishes a new investigation every week
It asks readers to suggest topics for research
qs.why: “what the reporters could not establish”

qs.q: What limitation of slow journalism is mentioned?
qs.a: It is unsuitable for events that need immediate coverage
w: It is too expensive for most readers to buy
It tends to ignore political stories
qs.why: “Nor can slow methods cover an emergency”

qs.q: What attitude does the writer show in the final sentence?
qs.a: Interest in the experiment despite an uncertain future
w: Confidence that slow journalism will replace fast news
Doubt that anyone will read such long articles
qs.why: “the fact that anyone is willing to bet on patience in this market is itself revealing.”

items.title: Science Without a Laboratory
items.tvi: Khoa học không cần phòng thí nghiệm
items.text:
When a rare dragonfly was recorded in a northern wetland last summer, the sighting did not come from a university team. It came from a retired bus driver with a camera and a free identification app. Such contributions are now central to what is called citizen science, in which volunteers collect data that professionals could never gather alone.

The advantages are considerable. Millions of observations from gardens, parks and coastlines provide a geographic spread that no research budget could match, and unusual patterns, such as birds arriving earlier each spring, are sometimes first noticed by amateurs. Some projects also seem to change the volunteers themselves: participants tend to report a stronger interest in conservation long after the survey has ended.

Scientists nonetheless handle the data with care. Volunteers photograph what is convenient, so common species near roads are heavily over-recorded while remote areas are neglected. Misidentification is another risk, which is why many projects require photographs and ask experts to verify unusual records. Statistical methods can correct some bias, though not all of it.

The most successful schemes, a coordinator observed, are those that give volunteers a role beyond collecting. When participants are shown how their records were used, and occasionally credited in published papers, they keep contributing for years. Where they are simply treated as a free workforce, enthusiasm fades quickly, and the data suffer accordingly. Respect, in other words, turns out to be a methodological issue as much as a moral one.

qs.q: What is the main advantage of citizen science?
qs.a: It collects observations over a very wide area
w: It costs scientists nothing to organise
It removes the need for expert checking
qs.why: “a geographic spread that no research budget could match”

qs.q: Why are the records not simply accepted as they are?
qs.a: Volunteers tend to record what is easy to reach
w: Volunteers often lose interest in the project
Photographs are too unclear to be useful
qs.why: “Volunteers photograph what is convenient”

qs.q: What does the coordinator say about successful schemes?
qs.a: They let volunteers see what their records achieved
w: They pay participants for their time
They limit projects to experienced observers
qs.why: “When participants are shown how their records were used”

qs.q: What does the final sentence imply?
qs.a: Treating volunteers well improves the quality of the research
w: Volunteers should be given more difficult tasks
Moral questions are more important than scientific ones
qs.why: “Respect, in other words, turns out to be a methodological issue as much as a moral one.”

items.title: In Defence of Nostalgia
items.tvi: Biện hộ cho nỗi nhớ về quá khứ
items.text:
Nostalgia was once classified as a disease. In the seventeenth century, physicians described it as a dangerous form of homesickness afflicting soldiers abroad, and prescribed remedies ranging from leeches to a return home. Today, psychologists take a very different view. Far from being a symptom of weakness, they suggest, nostalgia is a common emotional resource that most people draw on regularly.

Experiments point to several benefits. Recalling a fond memory can raise people's mood, reduce feelings of loneliness and even make them more willing to help strangers. Researchers believe that this is because nostalgic memories usually involve other people, reminding us that we belong to something larger than ourselves. Notably, the effect seems strongest when the memory is mixed, containing some sadness or loss alongside the happiness.

Yet there are reasons for caution. Nostalgia is selective, smoothing away the hardships of earlier times, and political movements have long exploited this by promising a return to a golden age that never quite existed. Marketing departments, too, have learned that familiar songs and old packaging can sell almost anything. A feeling that comforts the individual can, in other words, be used to manipulate the crowd.

The healthiest form of nostalgia, one psychologist suggests, is the kind that sends us forward: a person who remembers a close friendship may be prompted to phone the friend, rather than simply to sigh.

qs.q: How did seventeenth-century doctors view nostalgia?
qs.a: As a medical problem to be treated
w: As a sign of loyalty to one’s country
As a useful way of keeping soldiers calm
qs.why: “described it as a dangerous form of homesickness … and prescribed remedies”

qs.q: Why does recalling fond memories seem to help people?
qs.a: Such memories remind them of their connections to others
w: They help people forget unpleasant events
They make people more confident about the future
qs.why: “nostalgic memories usually involve other people”

qs.q: Why does the writer mention marketing departments?
qs.a: To show that nostalgia can be used to influence people
w: To explain why old songs are still popular
To prove that nostalgia is a modern invention
qs.why: “familiar songs and old packaging can sell almost anything.”

qs.q: What point is made by the psychologist's example of the friend?
qs.a: Nostalgia is most valuable when it leads to action
w: Nostalgia usually makes people sad
Friendships are the main cause of nostalgia
qs.why: “the kind that sends us forward”

items.title: Rethinking the Open-Plan Office
items.tvi: Nghĩ lại về văn phòng không vách ngăn
items.text:
Open-plan offices were promoted in the 1990s as spaces that would encourage conversation, spark ideas and flatten hierarchy. Walls came down, desks were pushed together, and companies saved on rent by fitting more people into less room. Three decades later, the evidence suggests that the promise was only partly kept.

A study of two firms that moved to open-plan layouts recorded a surprising result. Face-to-face interaction fell by roughly seventy per cent, while the use of email and messaging rose. Employees, it seems, responded to the lack of privacy by withdrawing: they put on headphones, avoided sensitive topics and sent a message to a colleague sitting two metres away rather than risk being overheard. Far from increasing spontaneous collaboration, the design appeared to discourage it.

Defenders of the format respond that results depend on how a space is used. Offices that include quiet rooms, small meeting areas and clear etiquette about noise perform better than those that simply remove the partitions. Younger staff, moreover, often report liking the energy of a shared floor, even when their concentration suffers.

The real lesson may be that no layout suits every task. Writing a report demands silence, while brainstorming profits from interruption. Companies that allow people to choose where to work according to the job, one consultant argues, are likely to find that flexibility matters more than architecture, and that the cheapest design is not necessarily the most productive.

qs.q: What was the original hope for open-plan offices?
qs.a: That they would increase conversation and new ideas
w: That they would make staff work longer hours
That they would reduce the need for managers
qs.why: “encourage conversation, spark ideas and flatten hierarchy”

qs.q: Why did face-to-face contact fall in the study?
qs.a: Staff sought privacy by avoiding being overheard
w: Staff had fewer meetings with managers
Staff were given less time to socialise
qs.why: “responded to the lack of privacy by withdrawing”

qs.q: What do defenders of open-plan offices claim?
qs.a: The outcome depends on how the space is organised
w: The study measured the wrong kind of contact
Younger employees are better at concentrating
qs.why: “results depend on how a space is used”

qs.q: What does 'the cheapest design is not necessarily the most productive' suggest?
qs.a: Saving money may have driven the trend more than evidence did
w: Open-plan offices are no longer cheap to build
Productivity cannot be measured in offices
qs.why: “the cheapest design is not necessarily the most productive.”

items.title: Do Tourist Taxes Work?
items.tvi: Thuế du lịch có hiệu quả không?
items.text:
As visitor numbers have soared, a growing number of cities have introduced tourist taxes, charging a small fee per night or per arrival. The measure is often presented as a way of making visitors contribute to the services they use, such as street cleaning and public transport.

Supporters point out that residents bear the costs of tourism without sharing in its profits. Local taxpayers pay for rubbish collection, while much of the money spent by visitors flows to international hotel chains and booking platforms. A modest levy, advocates say, redresses the balance at little cost to travellers, who rarely abandon a destination over a few euros.

Sceptics are not persuaded. Some economists argue that the fees are too small to reduce crowding, and that if reducing crowding is the real aim, caps on numbers or higher prices at peak times would be more effective. Others note that revenue is often absorbed into general budgets rather than spent on the visible problems. A hotel owner in one coastal town claimed, for example, that the tax had been in place for five years without a single new bench appearing on the seafront.

Where the policy appears to work best is where its purpose is clearly explained and the money is clearly spent. Visitors tend to accept a charge that funds a restored bridge more readily than one that vanishes into an unspecified account, a reminder that public trust depends on transparency as much as on the sums involved.

qs.q: How are tourist taxes usually justified?
qs.a: Visitors should help pay for services they use
w: They discourage people from visiting at all
They replace taxes paid by local residents
qs.why: “making visitors contribute to the services they use”

qs.q: Why do supporters think a small fee is acceptable?
qs.a: Travellers are unlikely to be put off by it
w: The fee goes directly to hotel owners
Residents are already paying higher prices
qs.why: “rarely abandon a destination over a few euros”

qs.q: What do some economists say about the fees?
qs.a: They are too low to ease overcrowding
w: They are too complicated to collect
They should be spent on advertising
qs.why: “the fees are too small to reduce crowding”

qs.q: Why does the writer mention the hotel owner?
qs.a: To illustrate doubts about how the money is used
w: To show that hotels oppose all taxes
To prove that the seafront was neglected before
qs.why: “without a single new bench appearing on the seafront.”

items.title: Why Urban Legends Endure
items.tvi: Vì sao truyền thuyết đô thị tồn tại lâu
items.text:
Every few years, a story circulates about a stranger who was drugged in a nightclub, or a pet that was dried in a microwave. Told with confidence by a friend of a friend, such tales spread quickly, even though they can rarely be traced to an actual event. Folklorists call them urban legends, and they argue that the question worth asking is not whether they are true but why they endure.

One explanation is that the stories carry a warning in disguise. A tale about a hitchhiker who turns out to be dangerous expresses a genuine anxiety about trusting strangers, packaged in a form that is easy to remember and retell. Researchers who have tested the way stories change as they pass between people found that details linked to disgust or fear survived far better than neutral ones, suggesting that the most alarming version tends to win.

The internet has not killed such legends; it has simply accelerated them. A rumour that once took months to cross a country can now cross it in an afternoon, often accompanied by a screenshot that seems to confirm it. Fact-checkers can disprove a claim within hours, yet the correction rarely travels as far as the original.

That asymmetry troubles scholars. A reassuring truth, it seems, is simply less shareable than a frightening falsehood, and anyone hoping to counter misinformation must first accept that people pass on stories for reasons that have little to do with accuracy.

qs.q: What do folklorists consider the important question about urban legends?
qs.a: Why the stories continue to spread
w: Who first invented each story
Which stories are true
qs.why: “not whether they are true but why they endure.”

qs.q: What does the hitchhiker story illustrate?
qs.a: A real worry expressed through a memorable tale
w: A crime that was widely reported
A warning invented by the police
qs.why: “expresses a genuine anxiety about trusting strangers”

qs.q: What did researchers find about how stories change?
qs.a: Frightening or disgusting details tend to last
w: Neutral details are the easiest to remember
Stories become shorter each time they are told
qs.why: “details linked to disgust or fear survived far better than neutral ones”

qs.q: What does the writer suggest is the main obstacle to countering rumours?
qs.a: People share stories for reasons other than accuracy
w: Fact-checkers work too slowly to be useful
Screenshots are impossible to verify
qs.why: “people pass on stories for reasons that have little to do with accuracy.”
